source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402
paragraph: High prevalence of developmental disorders that is affecting patient quality of life and is costly for society is a world-wide problem.1,2 The prevalence of developmental disorders diagnosed by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual version IV (DSM-IV) in Asia-Pacific regions was 39.2 in Australia, 16.1 in China, 181.1 in Japan and 189.0 in Korea (per 10 000 children).3–6

highlights.text: High prevalence of developmental disorders that is affecting patient quality of life and is costly for society is a world-wide problem.1,2

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402
paragraph: Children with developmental disorders commonly exhibit sleep disturbances that include difficulty settling into sleep, night waking and early morning waking.7–9 In particular, the prevalence of sleep disturbances among children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is higher than that among typical children.10 A report on 348 5-year-old children attending kindergarten or nursery school has suggested that greater irregularities in sleep–wake rhythms are associated with greater tendencies for problematic behaviours in children with ASD.11 Although sleep deprivation may occur at any age, adverse consequences are more likely to occur and persist in young children whose brains are rapidly developing than they are in adults.12 Although a causal association between ASD and sleep disturbance has not been definitively proven, reports show that children with ASD have dysfunctional γ-aminobutyric acid and melatonin, which are known to regulate sleep,13,14 and that their psychiatric symptoms may also interfere with sleep initiation.15 It is plausible that sleep deprivation aggravates problematic behaviours and has a negative impact on brain development.

highlights.text: In particular, the prevalence of sleep disturbances among children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is higher than that among typical children.10
It is plausible that sleep deprivation aggravates problematic behaviours and has a negative impact on brain development.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402
paragraph: Reports indicate that daytime physical activity (PA) is associated with the quantity and quality of sleep among healthy children and adolescents.16,17 For example, Foti et al. reported that greater than 60 min of daily PA led to sufficient sleep among high school children.16 In addition, Motegi et al. investigated the association between daytime PA and sleep among 4- to 6-year-old children using an accelerometer and demonstrated that high levels of PA during waking hours were associated with waking up spontaneously and in a good mood the following morning.18 However, whether similar associations holds true for children with ASD is still unclear. Because assessing whether high levels of daytime PA improves the sleep of ASD children is important, we investigated the association between daytime PA and the quantity and quality of sleep among pre-schoolers with ASD.

highlights.text: Reports indicate that daytime physical activity (PA) is associated with the quantity and quality of sleep among healthy children and adolescents.16,17

Because assessing whether high levels of daytime PA improves the sleep of ASD children is important, we investigated the association between daytime PA and the quantity and quality of sleep among pre-schoolers with ASD.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Participants
paragraph: Fifty-eight pre-school children (aged 48–83 months) were recruited from the developmental clinics at Osaka University Hospital from April 2011 to January 2012. All recruits had been diagnosed by developmental paediatricians to have ASD according to DSM-IV. Twenty-one control children (aged 48–83 months) with no histories of developmental disorders were recruited through a local nursery school from March 2011 to May 2011. Children were excluded if (i) they experienced adverse events during sleep measurement or PA (convulsive seizures, or catching a cold); (ii) they took off the measurement devices while playing sports; (iii) they did not complete measurements for seven consecutive days; or (iv) they did not complete the questionnaires. Subsequently, 31 children with ASD and 16 controls were included for further analysis.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Measures
paragraph: PA data were objectively measured using a small accelerometer (Actiwatch 2, Cambridge Neurotechnology Ltd., Cambridge, UK) worn on the non-dominant wrist for seven consecutive days, with a sampling rate of once per min. The Actiwatch has been reported as a valid and useful device for assessing daily PA in children19 and has been used to measure both sleep parameters and PA values in pre-school–aged children.20 Data were analysed with Sleep Analyses software (version 5, Cambridge Neurotechnology Ltd.) using a high sensitivity threshold level, and sleep onset, sleep-end time, total sleep duration (min), snooze time (min), sleep percentage and PA (counts/min) were calculated.21 Sleep onset was determined as the clock time corresponding to the first epoch of the first 10-min period of persistent sleep. Sleep-end time was the clock time corresponding to the last epoch of the last 10-min period of persistent sleep. Total sleep duration was calculated as the sum of sleep epochs between sleep onset and sleep-end time. Snooze time was defined as the time from sleep-end time to getting out of bed. Sleep percentage was defined as the percentage of total sleep time between sleep onset and sleep-end time. The parents of the participants recorded the times when their children removed the Actiwatch devices and when they put them back on (e.g. before and after taking a bath), and data from those periods were not included in the analysis (Fig. 1). Because the amount of PA could not be assessed when participants removed their Actiwatch devices while playing sports, we excluded those participants from the analysis (criteria #2 listed above).

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Measures
paragraph: Parents of the participants completed the Japanese version of the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) for 4- to 18-year-olds. The CBCL is made up of 113 questions categorised into the following eight subscales: (i) withdrawal; (ii) somatic complaints; (iii) anxiety/depression; (iv) social problems; (v) thought problems; (vi) attention problems; (vii) delinquent behaviours; and (viii) aggressive behaviours. Internalising (i + ii + iii), externalising (vii + viii) and total score were calculated and converted into t-scores. Higher scores indicate a stronger likelihood of problematic behaviours.22 Demographic information and subjective evaluations of participants’ sleep were obtained through a self-administered questionnaire completed by the parents of the participants. These subjective evaluations were based on a six-point scale: very good, good, somewhat good, somewhat poor, poor and very poor. Because of the small sample sizes, we categorised evaluations into either good or poor depending on which side of the scale they fell.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Statistical Analysis
paragraph: Differences in characteristics between control and ASD children were determined using a Mann–Whitney U-test. For each child and for each day, we calculated the average PA for three periods: 9:00 am to 12:00 pm (morning), 12:00 pm to 6:00 pm (afternoon) and 6:00 pm to sleep onset time (evening). We excluded the first measurement day from analysis in order to avoid the effect of the first night. In addition, we did not analyse the periods when participants took off their Actiwatch devices for more than 2 h. Between-person correlations between PA at these three periods and the sleep parameters were assessed by Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. Furthermore, we assessed within-person associations between PA and sleep at each period. The most active (with the highest PA value) and most inactive (with the lowest PA value) days were determined for each of these three periods (Fig. 1). We used a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the sleep indices following the most active morning, afternoon and evening of each subject with those following the most inactive periods.

highlights.text: Furthermore, we assessed within-person associations between PA and sleep at each period.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Statistical Analysis
paragraph: All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS statistical software (Version 19.0J; Japan IBM, Tokyo, Japan). All probability values were two-tailed with a significance level of P < 0.05.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Ethics Approval
paragraph: The Institutional Review Board of the Osaka University Hospital Ethics Committee approved this study. One of the authors (YT) explained the survey details to the parent(s) of the children and obtained written informed consent at the time of their visits.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Results
paragraph: Table 1 shows the characteristics of ASD and control children. All eight subscale items of the CBCL except for somatic complaints were significantly higher in ASD than in control children. Sleep percentage was significantly higher in controls (92.5%) than in ASD children (88.0%), and snooze time was significantly longer in ASD children (10.0 min) than in controls (8.0 min). The subjective evaluation by care givers revealed that the percentage of ‘poor’ sleepers was significantly higher in ASD children than in control children. Although PA did not differ between control and ASD children on weekdays, it was significantly lower on weekend mornings in ASD children. The coefficients of between-subject correlation between PA during any period and any sleep index are shown in Appendix I. There were no significant between-subject correlations in either control or ASD children.

highlights.text: Sleep percentage was significantly higher in controls (92.5%) than in ASD children (88.0%), and snooze time was significantly longer in ASD children (10.0 min) than in controls (8.0 min).
There were no significant between-subject correlations in either control or ASD children.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Results
paragraph: We further investigated intra-individual associations between PA and sleep. The most active morning and the most active afternoon occurred on the same day in five (31.3%) control children and nine (29.0%) ASD children. The most active morning, afternoon and evening occurred on the same day in only one (6.3%) control child and two (6.5%) ASD children. Similarly, whereas the most inactive morning and afternoon occurred on the same day in six (37.5%) control and five (16.1%) ASD children, the most inactive morning, afternoon and evening occurred on the same day in only one (6.3%) control child and two (6.5%) ASD children.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Results
paragraph: Table 2 shows sleep indices during the night following the days with the most active and inactive time periods. Sleep percentage for control children following the active morning was significantly higher (median: 93.2%) than that following the inactive morning (median: 91.7%), whereas sleep percentage in ASD children was not modulated by PA during any time period. Sleep onset for ASD children on the day of the active morning (median: 9:21 pm) was earlier than that on the day of the inactive morning (median: 9:57 pm), and this pattern was also true following the active (median: 9:39 pm) and the inactive (median: 10:24 pm) afternoons. In contrast, sleep onset in control children was not affected by PA during any time period. Neither group of children showed any other sleep index that was significantly affected by the amount of PA in evening. PA levels for the active and inactive periods are shown in Table 3. Differences in activity levels between active and inactive periods were not seasonal in nature (see Appendix II).

highlights.text: Sleep percentage for control children following the active morning was significantly higher (median: 93.2%) than that following the inactive morning (median: 91.7%), whereas sleep percentage in ASD children was not modulated by PA during any time period.

Sleep onset for ASD children on the day of the active morning (median: 9:21 pm) was earlier than that on the day of the inactive morning (median: 9:57 pm), and this pattern was also true following the active (median: 9:39 pm) and the inactive (median: 10:24 pm) afternoons.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: This is the first report investigating the effect of PA on the nocturnal sleep of pre-school–aged children with ASD. We found that compared with control children, ASD children exhibited poorer sleep on both objective and subjective measures. The key finding was that PA in the morning and afternoon resulted in earlier sleep onsets in ASD children and that PA in the morning resulted in significantly higher sleep percentages in control children.

highlights.text: The key finding was that PA in the morning and afternoon resulted in earlier sleep onsets in ASD children and that PA in the morning resulted in significantly higher sleep percentages in control children.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: Significant within-person associations were found between daytime PA and sleep schedule in ASD children. The earlier sleep onsets found in ASD children after daytime PA is sign of improvement, although the mechanism remains unknown. The serotonergic system, which has been reported to be impaired in ASD patients23 and which is activated through PA,24 may regulate circadian rhythms and sleep. Melatonin synthesis has been reported to improve difficulties in falling sleep but not to increase sleep percentage. Importantly, it has also been reported to be impaired in ASD patients. Thus, the earlier sleep onset in ASD children may have resulted from increased melatonin secretion.25,26 Consequently, daytime PA might regulate the circadian rhythms among ASD children through increased serotonin and melatonin secretion.

highlights.text: The earlier sleep onsets found in ASD children after daytime PA is sign of improvement, although the mechanism remains unknown.
Consequently, daytime PA might regulate the circadian rhythms among ASD children through increased serotonin and melatonin secretion.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: PA on weekend was significantly lower among ASD children compared with control children. ASD children (or their parents) likely engage in less outdoor activities than do normal children because ASD children can become upset or distressed by their disabilities during leisure activity27 and because their many problematic behaviours in unstructured outside settings may impose heavy burdens on their care givers. Indoor play such as watching television leads to irregular bedtimes.28 It is important to educate parents regarding the importance of regular outdoor activities for maintaining favourable sleep–wake cycles. Because earlier sleep onset was observed on weekdays, relatively high PA might improve sleep quality and quantity even if it is not excessive. The absence of significant between-person associations between daytime PA and sleep might indicate large individual differences in PA levels or in sleep quantity and quality. This may explain why the issue of it whether or not daytime PA is associated with the quality and quantity of sleep among healthy school-aged children is still controversial.7,18,29,30

highlights.text: It is important to educate parents regarding the importance of regular outdoor activities for maintaining favourable sleep–wake cycles.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: Many clinical trials have assessed the sleep of children with developmental disorders, and recent trials have reported the beneficial effects of melatonin on the quality and quantity of sleep for these children.31–34 However, we should bear in mind that PA might also be effective for children with sleep disturbances.

highlights.text: However, we should bear in mind that PA might also be effective for children with sleep disturbances.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: In contrast to ASD children, significant within-person associations between daytime PA and sleep percentage were found in control children, a fact also reported by Ekstedt et al.35 This association might be explained by Dworak et al., which showed that high-intensity exercise resulted in increased slow-wave sleep in the following night.36 The low prevalence of sleep disturbances among typical children compared with ASD children might indicate that typical children have fewer problems with circadian rhythms and may therefore fall asleep at a habitual time regardless of daytime PA. This might be one reason why daytime PA was not significantly associated with sleep schedule among control children. Although the reason why sleep percentage was not associated with morning or afternoon PA in ASD children remains to be clarified, the intrinsic deficit in sleep maintenance found in people suffering from ASD may explain this finding.10 Although daytime PA impacted different aspects of sleep in control and ASD children, high levels of daytime PA had positive effects on sleep for both groups.

highlights.text: Although daytime PA impacted different aspects of sleep in control and ASD children, high levels of daytime PA had positive effects on sleep for both groups.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: Evening PA was not associated with sleep quantity or quality in either group of children. Mindell et al. has reported that instituting a consistent nightly bedtime routine that includes a bath, a massage and quiet activities (e.g. cuddling and singing lullabies), with lights off within 30 min from the end of the bath, is beneficial in improving multiple aspects of infant sleep, especially wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep continuity.37 In addition, PA at night might affect nocturnal melatonin secretion, which is an important circadian indicator in humans, although the mechanism remains uncertain.38 Therefore, in contrast to morning and afternoon PA, PA in the evening might not lead to high sleep quantity or quality.

highlights.text: Evening PA was not associated with sleep quantity or quality in either group of children.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: Japanese infants and toddlers (0–36 months) were reported to have the lowest total amount of sleep among 17 countries in Asia, the Western Pacific, Europe, and North America.39 In addition, bedtime was relatively late: mean bedtimes (h) were 21.29 in Japan, 19.71 in Australia, 19.91 in UK and 20.87 in USA.39 Although these data came from participants who were not the same age as those in the present study, it is possible that Japanese children may also have less sleep and later bedtimes. Daytime PA might play an important role in improving sleep disturbances in Japanese children, regardless of whether or not they have developmental disorders.

highlights.text: Japanese infants and toddlers (0–36 months) were reported to have the lowest total amount of sleep among 17 countries in Asia, the Western Pacific, Europe, and North America.39
Daytime PA might play an important role in improving sleep disturbances in Japanese children, regardless of whether or not they have developmental disorders.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: The strengths of this study relate to the objectively measured PA and sleep data over multiple consecutive days. The Actiwatch is widely used in epidemiological research to measure sleep in an ecologically valid setting for the child.40 However, this study does have several limitations. First, the Actiwatch cannot assess static exercise and certain types of dynamic activities, such as cycling or tricycling.41,42 Second, the sample size was relatively small, especially for the control group. Third, measurements for the two groups were not conducted during the same season. Seasonal differences might affect sleep in children, which in turn might have affected the results. One argument against this, however, is that the differences in PA were independent of seasons (Appendix II). Finally, sleep was not evaluated by polysomnography, which can reveal sleep architecture and sleep quality. Future studies should research what kind of PA is most effective for good sleep and how daytime PA leads to improved sleep.

highlights.text: Second, the sample size was relatively small, especially for the control group.
Third, measurements for the two groups were not conducted during the same season.

source: Tatsumi et al. (2015). Daytime physical activity and sleep in pre-schoolers with developmental disorders. J Paediatr Child Health 51:396-402 — Discussion
paragraph: In conclusion, the associations between PA and the quality of sleep were different depending on when the PA occurred. High levels of morning and afternoon activity were associated with early sleep onset among ASD children. High-level morning and afternoon activity should be encouraged to improve the sleep quality of children with ASD.

highlights.text: High-level morning and afternoon activity should be encouraged to improve the sleep quality of children with ASD.
